This tutorial fits a connected pySEB structure to three real SANS datasets.
The sample is a water-in-cyclohexane microemulsion stabilized by an Aerosol
OT (AOT) surfactant layer. Isotopic substitution highlights the water core,
the complete droplet, or the surfactant shell while leaving the underlying
geometry unchanged.

The measurements are official
[SasData example data](https://www.sasview.org/docs/old_docs/6.1.0/user/example_data/testdata_help.html)
collected on the LOQ instrument at ISIS. The
[SasView simultaneous-fitting tutorial](https://www.sasview.org/downloads/simultaneous_1d_fitting_in_sasview_v6.pdf)
documents the sample, contrasts, scattering-length densities, and a more
complete analysis.

We start with a monodisperse, unsmeared baseline, then test size distributions,
interparticle interactions, and approximate instrumental resolution. Comparing
the fits and residuals shows which physical assumptions matter for these data.

## What you will fit

The structure contains two linked subunits:

```text
SolidSphere core.center = shell.center SolidSphericalShell

core radius = R
shell inner radius = R
shell outer radius = R + thickness
```

The three datasets share the core radius, shell thickness, and droplet volume
fraction. Their known contrasts change `beta_core` and `beta_shell`, and each
measurement receives its own flat background.

## Install the fitting dependency

Continue in the environment used for the introductory tutorials and add
SciPy and sasmodels:

```bash
python -m pip install "pyseb[sasmodels]" scipy
```

pySEB evaluates the scattering structure. SciPy's
[`least_squares`](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.optimize.least_squares.html)
adjusts bounded parameters to minimize the uncertainty-weighted residuals.

## 1. Load the measured data

The CSV files contain q in Å⁻¹, intensity in cm⁻¹, and the measured intensity
uncertainty. They are three-column extracts of the upstream CanSAS XML files;
no intensities have been synthesized or altered.

- [Core contrast data](data/aot-core-contrast.csv){download="aot-core-contrast.csv"}
- [Drop contrast data](data/aot-drop-contrast.csv){download="aot-drop-contrast.csv"}
- [Shell contrast data](data/aot-shell-contrast.csv){download="aot-shell-contrast.csv"}
- [SasData BSD-3-Clause license](data/SASDATA-LICENSE.txt){download="SASDATA-LICENSE.txt"}

```{python}
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pyseb
import sympy
from scipy.optimize import least_squares


data_directory = Path("data")
data_files = {
    "Core": data_directory / "aot-core-contrast.csv",
    "Drop": data_directory / "aot-drop-contrast.csv",
    "Shell": data_directory / "aot-shell-contrast.csv",
}

datasets = {}
for name, path in data_files.items():
    q, intensity, uncertainty = np.loadtxt(
        path, delimiter=",", skiprows=3, unpack=True
    )
    datasets[name] = {
        "q": q,
        "intensity": intensity,
        "uncertainty": uncertainty,
    }

print({name: data["q"].size for name, data in datasets.items()})
```

Each original dataset has 137 points. We use q ≤ 0.25 Å⁻¹ and require a
positive uncertainty. This removes the final high-q points where intensities
fluctuate around zero and one reported uncertainty is zero.

```{python}
for name, data in datasets.items():
    selected = (data["q"] <= 0.25) & (data["uncertainty"] > 0)
    for key in ("q", "intensity", "uncertainty"):
        data[key] = data[key][selected]

print({name: data["q"].size for name, data in datasets.items()})
```

## 2. Build the two-subunit structure

The shell and core are connected through their fixed `center` references.
Setting the shell's inner radius equal to the core radius makes the two
subunits occupy adjacent, non-overlapping volumes.

```{python}
def build_particle():
    world = pyseb.World("AOTMicroemulsionFit")
    droplet = world.Add("SolidSphere", "core")
    world.Link("SolidSphericalShell", "shell.center", "core.center")
    world.Add(droplet, "droplet")
    return world


world = build_particle()
```

Unlike a single preassembled core–shell function, this is an explicit pySEB
structure. Its total amplitude and core–shell interference follow from the
link between two reusable subunits.

### Inspect the generated form factor

`World.FormFactor()` returns the normalized symbolic expression assembled by
pySEB. Printing it here makes the equation being fitted inspectable rather
than hiding it behind the numerical evaluator.

```{python}
form_factor_expression = pyseb.SymPyExpression(
    str(world.FormFactor("droplet"))
).expr

print("Normalized pySEB form factor P(q) =")
print(form_factor_expression)
```

The printed expression is easier to read in factored form. Define
$x_c=qR$, $x_i=qR_i$, and $x_o=qR_o$:

$$
A_c(q)=3\frac{\sin(x_c)-x_c\cos(x_c)}{x_c^3},
$$

$$
A_s(q)=3\frac{x_i\cos(x_i)-x_o\cos(x_o)-\sin(x_i)+\sin(x_o)}
{x_o^3-x_i^3}.
$$

The normalized form factor generated by the linked structure is

$$
P(q)=\left[
\frac{\beta_c A_c(q)+\beta_s A_s(q)}{\beta_c+\beta_s}
\right]^2.
$$

Consequently, the unnormalized quantity used for the absolute-intensity fit
is

$$
I_{pySEB}(q)=(\beta_c+\beta_s)^2P(q)
             =[\beta_cA_c(q)+\beta_sA_s(q)]^2.
$$

::: {.callout-note title="Why use spheres here?"}
The source analysis treats these AOT droplets as spherical core–shell
particles, so a sphere is the parsimonious starting hypothesis. It has one
size coordinate, and pySEB provides an exact non-overlapping
`SolidSphere`–`SolidSphericalShell` construction.

A spheroid would introduce at least an equatorial radius, a polar radius, and
their associated distributions. More importantly, pySEB currently provides a
homogeneous `Spheroid` but no solid spheroidal-shell subunit. Simply linking
two homogeneous spheroids at their centers would create overlapping volumes
and would not by itself define a rigid, aligned core–shell spheroid. Testing
anisotropy properly therefore requires a `SolidSpheroidalShell` model (or an
equivalent aligned composite) followed by a fit-quality comparison that
justifies its extra parameters.
:::

## 3. Convert contrast into excess scattering length

The SLD values below are in units of 10⁻⁶ Å⁻² and are fixed from the SasView
tutorial. Each tuple contains core, shell, and solvent SLD.

```{python}
sld = {
    "Core": (6.39, 0.62, -0.28),
    "Drop": (-0.55, 0.62, 6.68),
    "Shell": (6.39, 0.62, 6.68),
}
```

For a homogeneous region, its excess scattering length is
$\beta=(\rho-\rho_{solvent})V$. The measured dilute-particle intensity is

$$
I(q)=\frac{\phi}{V_{total}} I_{pySEB}(q)10^8 + B,
$$

where $\phi$ is volume fraction, $I_{pySEB}$ is the unnormalized form factor
in Å², $10^8$ converts Å⁻¹ to cm⁻¹, and $B$ is a flat background.

```{python}
def calculate_intensity(
    contrast,
    q,
    core_radius,
    shell_thickness,
    volume_fraction,
    background,
):
    outer_radius = core_radius + shell_thickness
    core_volume = 4.0 * np.pi * core_radius**3 / 3.0
    total_volume = 4.0 * np.pi * outer_radius**3 / 3.0
    shell_volume = total_volume - core_volume

    core_sld, shell_sld, solvent_sld = sld[contrast]
    parameters = {
        "R_core": core_radius,
        "Ri_shell": core_radius,
        "Ro_shell": outer_radius,
        "beta_core": (
            (core_sld - solvent_sld) * 1e-6 * core_volume
        ),
        "beta_shell": (
            (shell_sld - solvent_sld) * 1e-6 * shell_volume
        ),
    }

    unnormalized = np.asarray(
        world.EvaluateFormFactorUnnormalized(
            "droplet", parameters, q.tolist()
        )
    )
    return (
        volume_fraction / total_volume * unnormalized * 1e8
        + background
    )
```

The signed betas are important. In core contrast, the shell is close to the
solvent match point, so the core dominates. In shell contrast, the core is
close to the solvent match point, so the shell dominates. Drop contrast
retains substantial scattering from both regions.

## 4. Define one simultaneous residual vector

The optimizer sees six independent fit parameters:

1. shared core radius;
2. shared shell thickness;
3. shared volume fraction;
4. core-contrast background;
5. drop-contrast background;
6. shell-contrast background.

::: {.callout-note title="This is already a multivariable fit"}
The radius, thickness, and volume fraction move together during optimization;
they are not fitted one at a time. The three backgrounds also move, giving six
fitted variables in total. Sharing the first three variables across all three
contrasts is what makes this a simultaneous fit.
:::

Every residual is divided by its measured uncertainty, so a value of two
means the calculation misses that point by two reported standard deviations.

```{python}
contrast_order = ("Core", "Drop", "Shell")


def residual_vector(values):
    core_radius, shell_thickness, volume_fraction = values[:3]
    backgrounds = values[3:]
    residuals = []

    for contrast, background in zip(contrast_order, backgrounds):
        data = datasets[contrast]
        prediction = calculate_intensity(
            contrast,
            data["q"],
            core_radius,
            shell_thickness,
            volume_fraction,
            background,
        )
        residuals.append(
            (prediction - data["intensity"]) / data["uncertainty"]
        )

    return np.concatenate(residuals)
```

## 5. Fit with physically useful bounds

The initial values are deliberately approximate. Bounds prevent negative
sizes, volume fractions, and backgrounds while still leaving a broad search
region.

```{python}
initial = np.array([20.0, 10.0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1])
lower = np.array([5.0, 1.0, 0.001, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0])
upper = np.array([60.0, 30.0, 0.2, 5.0, 5.0, 5.0])

fit = least_squares(
    residual_vector,
    initial,
    bounds=(lower, upper),
    x_scale="jac",
)

assert fit.success, fit.message

parameter_names = (
    "core radius (Å)",
    "shell thickness (Å)",
    "volume fraction",
    "core background (cm^-1)",
    "drop background (cm^-1)",
    "shell background (cm^-1)",
)
for name, value in zip(parameter_names, fit.x):
    print(f"{name:28s} {value:.6g}")

degrees_of_freedom = fit.fun.size - fit.x.size
reduced_chi_squared = np.sum(fit.fun**2) / degrees_of_freedom
print(f"reduced chi-squared         {reduced_chi_squared:.3f}")
```

The shared geometry is close to a 25 Å water core with an 8 Å surfactant
layer. The fitted volume fraction is close to 0.056. These are plausible
values, but the large reduced chi-squared warns that plausible parameters do
not by themselves establish an adequate model.

## 6. Plot data, fit, and normalized residuals

```{python}
#| label: fig-real-aot-simultaneous-fit
#| fig-cap: "Simultaneous baseline fit of the linked sphere-and-shell structure to three AOT microemulsion contrasts."

core_radius, shell_thickness, volume_fraction = fit.x[:3]
backgrounds = fit.x[3:]

figure, axes = plt.subplots(
    3, 2, figsize=(10, 10), sharex="col",
    gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.55, 1.0]},
)

for row, (contrast, background) in enumerate(
    zip(contrast_order, backgrounds)
):
    data = datasets[contrast]
    prediction = calculate_intensity(
        contrast,
        data["q"],
        core_radius,
        shell_thickness,
        volume_fraction,
        background,
    )
    normalized_residual = (
        data["intensity"] - prediction
    ) / data["uncertainty"]

    positive = data["intensity"] > 0
    axes[row, 0].errorbar(
        data["q"][positive],
        data["intensity"][positive],
        yerr=data["uncertainty"][positive],
        fmt=".",
        markersize=3,
        label="measurement",
    )
    axes[row, 0].plot(data["q"], prediction, label="pySEB fit")
    axes[row, 0].set_xscale("log")
    axes[row, 0].set_yscale("log")
    axes[row, 0].set_ylabel(f"{contrast}\n$I(q)$ (cm$^{{-1}}$)")
    axes[row, 0].legend(fontsize="small")

    axes[row, 1].plot(data["q"], normalized_residual, ".", markersize=3)
    axes[row, 1].axhline(0.0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
    axes[row, 1].axhline(2.0, color="grey", linewidth=0.6, linestyle="--")
    axes[row, 1].axhline(-2.0, color="grey", linewidth=0.6, linestyle="--")
    axes[row, 1].set_xscale("log")
    axes[row, 1].set_ylabel("residual / uncertainty")

axes[-1, 0].set_xlabel(r"$q$ (Å$^{-1}$)")
axes[-1, 1].set_xlabel(r"$q$ (Å$^{-1}$)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Random residuals scattered mostly between -2 and +2 would support the model.
Instead, long runs of positive and negative residuals remain, especially for
drop and shell contrast. The optimizer converged; the physical model is what
needs improvement.

## 7. Improve the model with size distributions

The baseline assumes that every droplet has exactly the same core radius and
shell thickness. Real microemulsions contain a distribution of sizes. We now
fit two more shared variables:

7. relative standard deviation of the core radius;
8. relative standard deviation of the shell thickness.

The core radius uses a positive log-normal distribution. The shell thickness
uses a normal distribution truncated at zero, because a negative thickness is
not physical. Both are number distributions: each sampled droplet contributes
according to its probability, and the absolute intensity uses the population's
mean total volume.

Evaluating dozens of sizes through the high-level pySEB API on every optimizer
step would be unnecessarily slow. Instead, ask pySEB for the structure's
symbolic form factor and amplitude once, then let sasmodels compile and
average them. The fitted equation still comes from the same two-subunit
pySEB graph.

```{python}
normalized_expression = form_factor_expression

(
    q_symbol,
    core_radius_symbol,
    shell_inner_symbol,
    shell_outer_symbol,
    beta_core_symbol,
    beta_shell_symbol,
) = sympy.symbols(
    "q R_core Ri_shell Ro_shell beta_core beta_shell"
)

unnormalized_expression = normalized_expression * (
    beta_core_symbol + beta_shell_symbol
) ** 2

```

### Let sasmodels average the pySEB particle

We expose the amplitude generated by our linked pySEB structure as a sasmodels
`Fq` model. sasmodels will handle size distributions and volume normalization.
The particle expression still comes from pySEB. For this spherical particle,
the squared center amplitude equals its form factor; this does not hold in
general for anisotropic or flexible structures.

The optional `pyseb.sasmodels` adapter generates a CPU kernel from that
expression to keep repeated fitting evaluations fast. A C compiler is needed on first use;
OpenCL and the SasView desktop application are not required.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Connect the pySEB expression to sasmodels"
from functools import lru_cache

from sasmodels.core import build_model
from sasmodels.direct_model import call_Fq, call_kernel
from sasmodels.resolution import Perfect1D, Pinhole1D
from pyseb.sasmodels import (
    Parameter, ModelSpec, InteractionSpec, SymbolicSpec,
    make_model_info, with_hardsphere, positive_gaussian,
)


def bind_particle(world, values):
    radius, thickness = values["radius"], values["thickness"]
    vc = 4 * np.pi * radius**3 / 3
    vo = 4 * np.pi * (radius + thickness)**3 / 3
    return dict(
        R_core=radius, Ri_shell=radius, Ro_shell=radius + thickness,
        beta_core=(values["sld_core"] - values["sld_solvent"]) * 1e-6 * vc,
        beta_shell=(values["sld_shell"] - values["sld_solvent"]) * 1e-6 * (vo - vc),
    )


# These substitutions declare the same parameter mapping for the optional
# generated analytical backend. Runtime clouds/hybrids need only bind_particle.
radius, thickness, rc, rs, solvent = sympy.symbols(
    "radius thickness sld_core sld_shell sld_solvent"
)
vc = 4 * sympy.pi * radius**3 / 3
vo = 4 * sympy.pi * (radius + thickness)**3 / 3
signed_expression = sympy.cancel(sympy.sympify(
    str(world.FormFactorAmplitude("droplet:core.center"))
) * (beta_core_symbol + beta_shell_symbol))

particle_spec = ModelSpec(
    name="pyseb_aot", world_factory=build_particle, structure="droplet",
    bind=bind_particle, intensity_factor=1e8,
    parameters=[
        Parameter("radius", 25., (0., np.inf), "Ang", "Core radius", True),
        Parameter("thickness", 8., (0., np.inf), "Ang", "Shell thickness", True),
        Parameter("sld_core", 6.39, units="1e-6/Ang^2"),
        Parameter("sld_shell", .62, units="1e-6/Ang^2"),
        Parameter("sld_solvent", -.28, units="1e-6/Ang^2"),
    ],
    volume=lambda p: 4 * np.pi * (p["radius"] + p["thickness"])**3 / 3,
    volume_parameters=("radius", "thickness"),
    interaction=InteractionSpec(
        "droplet:core.center", lambda p: p["radius"] + p["thickness"],
    ),
    symbolic=SymbolicSpec(
        parameters=dict(R_core=radius, Ri_shell=radius, Ro_shell=radius+thickness,
                        beta_core=(rc-solvent)*sympy.Rational(1, 10**6)*vc,
                        beta_shell=(rs-solvent)*sympy.Rational(1, 10**6)*(vo-vc)),
        volume=vo, amplitude=signed_expression, effective_radius=radius+thickness,
    ),
)
particle_info = make_model_info(particle_spec, backend="compiled")
particle_model = build_model(particle_info, platform="dll", dtype="double")
positive_thickness_distribution = positive_gaussian()


@lru_cache(maxsize=16)
def particle_kernel(q_values):
    return particle_model.make_kernel([np.asarray(q_values)])


def population_parameters(contrast, radius, thickness, radius_sd, thickness_sd,
                          population_points=41):
    core_sld, shell_sld, solvent_sld = sld[contrast]
    sigma_log = np.sqrt(np.log1p(radius_sd**2))
    return dict(
        # sasmodels lognormal center is the median; width is sigma(log R).
        radius=radius * np.exp(-sigma_log**2 / 2), radius_pd=sigma_log,
        radius_pd_type="lognormal", radius_pd_n=population_points,
        radius_pd_nsigma=8.0,
        thickness=thickness, thickness_pd=thickness_sd,
        thickness_pd_type=positive_thickness_distribution, thickness_pd_n=population_points,
        thickness_pd_nsigma=8.0,
        sld_core=core_sld, sld_shell=shell_sld, sld_solvent=solvent_sld,
    )


def calculate_disperse_intensity(contrast, q, core_radius, shell_thickness,
                               core_relative_sd, shell_relative_sd,
                               volume_fraction, background,
                               population_points=41):
    parameters = population_parameters(
        contrast, core_radius, shell_thickness,
        core_relative_sd, shell_relative_sd, population_points,
    )
    return call_kernel(particle_kernel(tuple(q)), dict(
        parameters, scale=volume_fraction, background=background,
    ))
```

`radius` in the fit remains the arithmetic mean and its width remains the
coefficient of variation; the adapter converts these into sasmodels'
lognormal median and log-space width. Shell thickness and width describe the
underlying normal distribution, truncated at positive thickness. sasmodels
samples both distributions on finite grids. A small custom dispersion class
uses smooth positive-thickness nodes: the built-in Gaussian drops grid points
at zero thickness, which can introduce jumps while fitting broad distributions.
The adapter's `positive_gaussian()` extension supplies nodes and weights;
sasmodels performs the averaging.
We check both grids for convergence below.
Its kernel uses amplitudes multiplied by $10^4$ and squared amplitudes by
$10^8$, so a volume-fraction scale gives intensity in cm⁻¹.

Fit the eight variables simultaneously. The initial geometry, volume fraction,
and backgrounds come from the monodisperse fit; only the two distribution
widths are new guesses.

```{python}
def disperse_residual_vector(values):
    (
        core_radius,
        shell_thickness,
        core_relative_sd,
        shell_relative_sd,
        volume_fraction,
    ) = values[:5]
    residuals = []

    for contrast, background in zip(contrast_order, values[5:]):
        data = datasets[contrast]
        prediction = calculate_disperse_intensity(
            contrast,
            data["q"],
            core_radius,
            shell_thickness,
            core_relative_sd,
            shell_relative_sd,
            volume_fraction,
            background,
        )
        residuals.append(
            (prediction - data["intensity"]) / data["uncertainty"]
        )

    return np.concatenate(residuals)


disperse_initial = np.concatenate(
    (fit.x[:2], [0.12, 0.42], fit.x[2:])
)
disperse_lower = np.array(
    [5.0, 1.0, 0.01, 0.01, 0.001, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
)
disperse_upper = np.array(
    [60.0, 30.0, 0.5, 0.8, 0.2, 5.0, 5.0, 5.0]
)

disperse_fit = least_squares(
    disperse_residual_vector,
    disperse_initial,
    bounds=(disperse_lower, disperse_upper),
    x_scale="jac",
)

assert disperse_fit.success, disperse_fit.message

disperse_parameter_names = (
    "core radius (Å)",
    "shell thickness (Å)",
    "core relative SD",
    "shell relative SD",
    "volume fraction",
    "core background (cm^-1)",
    "drop background (cm^-1)",
    "shell background (cm^-1)",
)
for name, value in zip(disperse_parameter_names, disperse_fit.x):
    print(f"{name:28s} {value:.6g}")

disperse_degrees_of_freedom = (
    disperse_fit.fun.size - disperse_fit.x.size
)
disperse_reduced_chi_squared = (
    np.sum(disperse_fit.fun**2) / disperse_degrees_of_freedom
)
print(f"baseline reduced chi-squared {reduced_chi_squared:.3f}")
print(
    "disperse reduced chi-squared "
    f"{disperse_reduced_chi_squared:.3f}"
)
```

| Quantity | Monodisperse fit | Size-distribution fit | SasView tutorial |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Core radius | 24.75 Å | 23.74 Å | about 23.5 Å |
| Shell thickness | 8.29 Å | 7.11 Å | about 7.3 Å |
| Core relative SD | — | 0.106 | about 0.12 |
| Shell relative SD | — | 0.438 | about 0.42 |
| Reduced chi-squared | 29.50 | 20.49 | not reported |

The fitted distribution widths are genuine optimizer variables, not values
copied from the [SasView tutorial](https://www.sasview.org/downloads/simultaneous_1d_fitting_in_sasview_v6.pdf).
Their proximity to that independent analysis is a useful check, not proof that
the model is complete.

## 8. Compare the improved fit

```{python}
#| label: fig-real-aot-disperse-fit
#| fig-cap: "Adding fitted core-radius and shell-thickness distributions improves all three contrasts. The dashed line is the monodisperse baseline."

(
    core_radius,
    shell_thickness,
    core_relative_sd,
    shell_relative_sd,
    volume_fraction,
) = disperse_fit.x[:5]
backgrounds = disperse_fit.x[5:]

figure, axes = plt.subplots(
    3, 2, figsize=(10, 10), sharex="col",
    gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.55, 1.0]},
)

for row, (contrast, background) in enumerate(
    zip(contrast_order, backgrounds)
):
    data = datasets[contrast]
    prediction = calculate_disperse_intensity(
        contrast,
        data["q"],
        core_radius,
        shell_thickness,
        core_relative_sd,
        shell_relative_sd,
        volume_fraction,
        background,
    )
    baseline_prediction = calculate_intensity(
        contrast,
        data["q"],
        fit.x[0],
        fit.x[1],
        fit.x[2],

        data["intensity"] - prediction

        markersize=3,

    axes[row, 0].plot(
        data["q"], baseline_prediction,

    axes[row, 0].set_xscale("log")
    axes[row, 0].set_yscale("log")
    axes[row, 0].set_ylabel(f"{contrast}\n$I(q)$ (cm$^{{-1}}$)")
    axes[row, 0].legend(fontsize="small")

    axes[row, 1].plot(data["q"], normalized_residual, ".", markersize=3)
    axes[row, 1].axhline(0.0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
    axes[row, 1].axhline(2.0, color="grey", linewidth=0.6, linestyle="--")
    axes[row, 1].axhline(-2.0, color="grey", linewidth=0.6, linestyle="--")
    axes[row, 1].set_xscale("log")
    axes[row, 1].set_ylabel("residual / uncertainty")

axes[-1, 0].set_xlabel(r"$q$ (Å$^{-1}$)")
axes[-1, 1].set_xlabel(r"$q$ (Å$^{-1}$)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The extra variables reduce the systematic mismatch and bring the geometry
close to the more complete SasView analysis. They do not make the residuals
random or reduce the reduced chi-squared to approximately one. The official
analysis also applies an approximate 10% $dQ/Q$ LOQ resolution smearing
correction and still describes its result as imperfect.

## 9. Account for interactions between droplets

This is an optional extension to the basic pySEB fitting workflow. pySEB
supplies the linked particle's scattering expression; sasmodels supplies
interactions and resolution, and SciPy fits the parameters. sasmodels also averages the particle population. The adapter connects these
components through the optional `pyseb.sasmodels` interface. The fitting
choices remain explicit in this tutorial. See the
[sasmodels resolution API](https://www.sasview.org/docs/dev/sasmodels-api/resolution.html)
for the measurement interface.

Size distributions smooth the form-factor minima, but do not account for
correlations between droplet positions. At a volume fraction around 6%,
the dilute-particle assumption deserves a test. A
[Percus–Yevick hard-sphere structure factor](https://www.sasview.org/docs/user/models/hardsphere.html)
provides a simple model of excluded-volume repulsion.

For a polydisperse population we use the **decoupling approximation**:

$$
I(q)=\frac{\phi}{\langle V\rangle}10^8
\left[\langle F(q)^2\rangle+
\langle F(q)\rangle^2\{S(q)-1\}\right]+B.
$$

Here $F=\beta_c A_c+\beta_s A_s$ is the signed amplitude of our linked
structure. Averaging the signed amplitude matters: simply multiplying the
averaged intensity by $S(q)$ neglects the contrast-dependent correction for
size dispersity. This approximation neglects correlations between particle
size and position; it is not an exact mixture structure factor.

We add one shared parameter, the effective interaction packing fraction
$\eta$. The hard-sphere radius is fixed to
$(3\langle V\rangle/4\pi)^{1/3}$. We keep $\eta$ separate from the absolute
intensity's volume fraction $\phi$: this tests an effective interaction model,
not a strictly self-consistent hard-sphere fluid. A successful fit does not
establish a microscopic interaction potential.

We also include a fixed Gaussian resolution with standard deviation
$\sigma_q=0.10q$, following the approximate resolution assumed in the
[source tutorial](https://www.sasview.org/downloads/simultaneous_1d_fitting_in_sasview_v6.pdf).
The files contain no measured resolution widths, so this remains an assumption.
We use sasmodels `Pinhole1D` with its default finite Gaussian window
(2.5 standard deviations below and 3 above each measured q), rather than an
unbounded Gaussian convolution.
Resolution is applied to the complete interacting intensity before comparison
with the data. All 363 selected measurements and their original uncertainties
remain in the objective.

### Evaluate the population and structure factor

sasmodels composes our particle with `hardsphere`. We explicitly select
`structure_factor_mode=1` for the decoupling approximation. Its product model
normally uses the same volume fraction for interaction strength and absolute
intensity. Here the effective packing fraction remains independent: we set
`volfraction=eta` and `scale=phi/eta`. At zero eta we use the particle directly.
The effective radius is calculated from the library's averaged particle volume,
preserving the radius convention used above.

```{python}
interaction_info = with_hardsphere(particle_spec, backend="compiled")
interaction_model = build_model(interaction_info, platform="dll", dtype="double")


@lru_cache(maxsize=16)
def interaction_kernel(q_values):
    return interaction_model.make_kernel([np.asarray(q_values)])


@lru_cache(maxsize=16)
def measurement_resolution(q_values, resolution_points=3000):
    q = np.asarray(q_values)
    q_calc = np.geomspace(0.7 * q.min(), 1.4 * q.max(), resolution_points)
    return Pinhole1D(q, 0.10 * q, q_calc=q_calc)


def interacting_intensity(contrast, q, values, background,
                          population_points=41, resolution_points=3000):
    radius, thickness, radius_sd, thickness_sd, phi = values[:5]
    eta = values[8]
    parameters = population_parameters(
        contrast, radius, thickness, radius_sd, thickness_sd, population_points,
    )
    resolution = measurement_resolution(tuple(q), resolution_points)
    if eta == 0:
        theory = call_kernel(particle_kernel(tuple(resolution.q_calc)), dict(
            parameters, scale=phi, background=0.0,
        ))
    else:
        _, _, _, mean_volume, _ = call_Fq(
            particle_kernel((0.01,)), parameters.copy(),
        )
        theory = call_kernel(interaction_kernel(tuple(resolution.q_calc)), dict(
            parameters, radius_effective=(3 * mean_volume / (4 * np.pi))**(1/3),
            volfraction=eta, scale=phi/eta, background=0.0,
            structure_factor_mode=1, radius_effective_mode=0,
        ))
    return resolution.apply(theory) + background
```

### Fit the same data with one additional variable

```{python}
def interacting_residual_vector(values, **quadrature):
    return np.concatenate([
        (interacting_intensity(
            contrast, datasets[contrast]["q"], values, values[5 + index],
            **quadrature,
        ) - datasets[contrast]["intensity"]) / datasets[contrast]["uncertainty"]
        for index, contrast in enumerate(contrast_order)
    ])


interaction_lower = np.r_[disperse_lower, 0.0]
interaction_upper = np.r_[disperse_upper, 0.3]
interaction_fit = least_squares(
    interacting_residual_vector,
    np.r_[disperse_fit.x, 0.05],
    bounds=(interaction_lower, interaction_upper),
    x_scale="jac",
)
assert interaction_fit.success, interaction_fit.message
interaction_chi_squared = np.sum(interaction_fit.fun**2) / (
    interaction_fit.fun.size - interaction_fit.x.size
)
for name, value in zip(
    (*disperse_parameter_names, "interaction packing fraction"), interaction_fit.x,
):
    print(f"{name:30s} {value:.6g}")
print(f"interacting reduced chi-squared {interaction_chi_squared:.3f}")

for label, result in (
    ("monodisperse", fit), ("size distributions", disperse_fit),
    ("interactions + resolution", interaction_fit),
):
    chi2 = np.sum(result.fun**2)
    print(f"{label:26s} k={result.x.size:2d}  "
          f"chi2/dof={chi2 / (result.fun.size - result.x.size):.3f}  "
          f"AIC={chi2 + 2 * result.x.size:.1f}")
```

AIC here omits the common constant for independent Gaussian observations with
known uncertainties. It penalizes added parameters, but a lower AIC does not
prove the model is physically correct.

### Check numerical accuracy and inspect the residuals

We compare the adapter with an independent sasmodels core-shell model at
all three contrasts, check the zero-dispersity and zero-interaction limits,
and double the distribution and resolution grids. Integration error should
be small compared with the measured uncertainties.

```{python}
from sasmodels.core import load_model

check_q = datasets["Core"]["q"]
reference_model = load_model("core_shell_sphere", platform="dll", dtype="double")
reference_kernel = reference_model.make_kernel([check_q])
for index, contrast in enumerate(contrast_order):
    parameters = population_parameters(contrast, *interaction_fit.x[:4])
    expected = call_kernel(reference_kernel, dict(parameters, scale=1., background=0.))
    actual = call_kernel(particle_kernel(tuple(check_q)), dict(parameters, scale=1., background=0.))
    np.testing.assert_allclose(actual, expected, rtol=1e-7, atol=1e-8)

    radius, thickness = interaction_fit.x[:2]
    rc, rs, solvent = sld[contrast]
    vc = 4 * np.pi * radius**3 / 3
    vo = 4 * np.pi * (radius + thickness)**3 / 3
    native = world.EvaluateFormFactorUnnormalized("droplet", {
        "R_core": radius, "Ri_shell": radius, "Ro_shell": radius + thickness,
        "beta_core": (rc-solvent)*1e-6*vc,
        "beta_shell": (rs-solvent)*1e-6*(vo-vc),
    }, check_q.tolist())
    mono = calculate_disperse_intensity(contrast, check_q, radius, thickness, 0, 0, 1, 0)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(mono, np.asarray(native)*1e8/vo, rtol=1e-7, atol=1e-8)

    tiny_eta = interaction_fit.x.copy()
    tiny_eta[8] = 1e-10
    zero_eta = interaction_fit.x.copy()
    zero_eta[8] = 0
    resolution = measurement_resolution(tuple(check_q))
    unsmeared = calculate_disperse_intensity(contrast, resolution.q_calc, *zero_eta[:5], 0.)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(interacting_intensity(contrast, check_q, zero_eta, 0.),
                               resolution.apply(unsmeared), rtol=1e-12)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(interacting_intensity(contrast, check_q, tiny_eta, 0.),
                               resolution.apply(unsmeared), rtol=1e-8)
reference_kernel.release()
reference_model.release()
np.testing.assert_allclose(resolution.apply(np.ones_like(resolution.q_calc)), 1)
np.testing.assert_allclose(Perfect1D(check_q).apply(check_q**2), check_q**2)
fine_residual = interacting_residual_vector(
    interaction_fit.x, population_points=81, resolution_points=6000,
)
disperse_fine = np.concatenate([
    (calculate_disperse_intensity(
        contrast, datasets[contrast]["q"], *disperse_fit.x[:5],
        disperse_fit.x[5 + index], population_points=81,
    ) - datasets[contrast]["intensity"]) / datasets[contrast]["uncertainty"]
    for index, contrast in enumerate(contrast_order)
])
assert np.max(np.abs(disperse_fine - disperse_fit.fun)) < 0.05
quadrature_error = np.max(np.abs(fine_residual - interaction_fit.fun))
print(f"Largest integration change / measured uncertainty: {quadrature_error:.4g}")
assert quadrature_error < 0.05
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-real-aot-interacting-fit
#| fig-cap: "Shared geometry with hard-sphere interactions and approximate resolution smearing. Dashed curves show the noninteracting size-distribution fit."

figure, axes = plt.subplots(3, 2, figsize=(10, 10), sharex="col")
for index, contrast in enumerate(contrast_order):
    data = datasets[contrast]
    prediction = interacting_intensity(
        contrast, data["q"], interaction_fit.x, interaction_fit.x[5 + index],
    )
    previous = calculate_disperse_intensity(
        contrast, data["q"], *disperse_fit.x[:5], disperse_fit.x[5 + index],
    )
    positive = data["intensity"] > 0
    axes[index, 0].errorbar(
        data["q"][positive], data["intensity"][positive],
        yerr=data["uncertainty"][positive], fmt=".", markersize=3,
        label="measurement",
    )
    axes[index, 0].plot(data["q"], previous, "--", color="grey", label="noninteracting")
    axes[index, 0].plot(data["q"], prediction, label="interactions + resolution")
    axes[index, 0].set(xscale="log", yscale="log", ylabel=f"{contrast}\n$I(q)$ (cm$^{{-1}}$)")
    axes[index, 0].legend(fontsize="small")
    residual = (data["intensity"] - prediction) / data["uncertainty"]
    axes[index, 1].plot(data["q"], residual, ".", markersize=3)
    for level in (-2, 0, 2):
        axes[index, 1].axhline(level, color="grey", linewidth=0.7)
    axes[index, 1].set(xscale="log", ylabel="residual / uncertainty")
    print(f"{contrast}: mean squared normalized residual = {np.mean(residual**2):.3f}")
for axis in axes[-1]:
    axis.set_xlabel(r"$q$ (Å$^{-1}$)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The reduced chi-squared falls from **29.50** for the monodisperse model to
**20.49** with size distributions and **1.83** with interactions and sasmodels resolution.
The final fit has nine parameters, compared with eight for the noninteracting
size-distribution model. The core radius is about **25.2 Å**, shell thickness
**8.6 Å**, core relative width **0.158**, and shell relative width **0.366**.
The shared volume fraction is about **0.0596** and effective interaction packing
fraction about **0.0762**.

This comparison adds interactions and resolution together. It demonstrates
their combined effect; it does not establish how much of the improvement
comes from either contribution separately.

The shell-contrast background reaches its lower bound of zero. Residuals still
show some mismatch, and the resolution was assumed rather than measured. These
are reasons to avoid treating the fitted geometry as a unique solution or
reporting precision based only on the optimizer's local curvature. The next
experimental checks would be measured resolution, background subtraction, and
whether the same interaction model is adequate at other concentrations.

## What this demonstrates

- A fit can use an explicit linked pySEB structure rather than a single
  preassembled subunit.
- Contrast variation changes signed scattering weights while sharing the same
  structure geometry.
- `EvaluateFormFactorUnnormalized` connects subunit betas to absolute-scale
  intensity.
- pySEB's generated particle expression can be compiled once and exposed to
  sasmodels for population averaging and absolute-volume normalization.
- Simultaneous residuals enforce shared physical parameters across datasets.
- sasmodels composes the particle with a structure factor; its beta mode
  uses the signed mean amplitude for the dispersity correction.
- Resolution convolution and integration-convergence checks are part of the
  forward model.
- A successful optimizer and plausible parameters do not guarantee a good
  scattering model.
